An override is what happens when something with more authority steps in and cancels, replaces, or takes precedence over something that was already in place — a rule, a decision, an automatic process, or a setting that was previously running things.

Think of it this way. Imagine a fire alarm is connected to a system that automatically locks every door in a building the moment it goes off. One day, a fire breaks out, but the automatic door-locking system malfunctions and traps people inside. A security officer then uses a special control panel to release all the doors manually. That action — and the control panel itself — can both be called an override. The officer didn't change the system permanently. They overruled it in that moment, with higher authority.

This is the soul of the word: an override doesn't just alter something. It asserts that something else takes priority over what was already decided or already running.

As a device or mechanism. This is the most physical sense of the word. Here, an override is a specific button, switch, key, or control that exists for the express purpose of bypassing an automatic or lower-level system. When you use it, you are telling the machine: "Stop following your automatic instructions. I am taking control."

"The autopilot failed during the storm, so the pilot used the manual override to regain control of the plane."

You'll see this sense everywhere in mechanical and digital systems — aircraft, elevators, factory machinery, nuclear reactors, car safety systems, and security systems all typically have some form of manual override built in. It is a designed escape hatch: a way for a human (or a higher system) to step above the automated logic when needed. The very existence of an override built into a system is an acknowledgment that no automation should be completely beyond human control.

As an act or event. "Override" can also refer to the moment or act itself — the event of one authority canceling what another had put in place.

The clearest real-world example is a veto override in politics. In the United States, when a president rejects (vetoes) a bill, Congress can fight back by voting to pass it anyway. If two-thirds of Congress votes in favor, the president's rejection is defeated. That act — Congress successfully defeating the president's veto — is called an override or a veto override.

"The Senate's veto override was a historic moment. The bill became law despite the president's objections."

You will also hear this sense used more loosely in everyday language. "Her last-minute decision was an override of everything the committee had already agreed upon." Here, override means the act of one person's authority canceling out a group's prior decision.

As a setting or instruction in software. In computing and software, an override is a piece of code, configuration, or instruction that replaces a default or inherited behavior. The key idea is that a system has a rule set at a general level, and the override is a more specific instruction that says: "For this particular case, ignore the general rule and do this instead."

A simple example: a website may have a global rule that all text should appear in black. But one specific page might have an override instruction that makes its text appear in dark blue. The global rule still exists; the override simply takes precedence for that specific page.

In object-oriented programming — a style of writing software — an override is when a child class (a more specific version of a program component) rewrites a behavior it inherited from its parent class. The child's version takes priority over the parent's. "The subclass had an override for that method, which is why it behaved differently than expected."

As a financial payment in sales. In business, particularly in sales organizations, an override (sometimes called an overriding commission) is a percentage of earnings that a manager or senior figure receives based on the sales made by the people they manage — on top of any commissions they earn from their own sales.

"As the regional director, she earned a 5% override on every deal her team closed."

The logic connects back to the core idea: the manager's compensation "sits above" the standard commission structure. It is a layer of earnings derived from a position of authority over others.
The one thread that connects every meaning

Whether an override is a button on a control panel, a congressional vote, a line of code, or a management commission, the word always points to the same essential dynamic: there is something already in place — a rule, a system, a decision, a default — and something with higher authority, more urgency, or more specificity comes along and supersedes it.

An override is never accidental and never passive. It is always a deliberate assertion that one thing takes precedence over another. When you hear or read the word, always ask yourself: what was already in place, and what is overruling it? The answer to those two questions will unlock the full meaning in any context.

In conversations and texts, you will most often see "override" as a noun in these combinations: a manual override (a physical control to bypass automation), a veto override (a legislature defeating an executive's rejection), an override code or override key (a special code that bypasses a lock or security measure), a commission override (extra earnings for a manager based on their team's performance), and a configuration override or CSS override (a software setting that replaces a default rule).

Each of these phrases follows the same pattern: the word before "override" tells you what kind of thing is being superseded, and the override itself is what comes in to supersede it.
